sub: Why the uptake scan separates a gland that is overmaking hormone from one that is leaking it.

pretest.q: Radioactive iodine uptake is low in a thyrotoxic patient. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Release of stored hormone from an inflamed gland
Stimulating antibodies at the TSH receptor
pretest.why: Low uptake means the gland is not making new hormone: stored hormone is leaking from damaged follicles, as in subacute or painless thyroiditis, or hormone is exogenous.

w.Stimulating antibodies at the TSH recept: Graves antibodies drive synthesis, so uptake is diffusely high, not low.
w.A toxic adenoma: An autonomous nodule takes up iodine avidly and appears as a hot nodule with the rest of the gland suppressed.
w.A TSH-secreting adenoma: Excess TSH drives the whole gland to make hormone, so uptake is high and TSH is inappropriately normal or high.

body: Making too much or leaking too much

Thyrotoxicosis has two broad causes. The gland can **overproduce** hormone, as in Graves disease or a toxic nodule, and then radioactive iodine uptake is high. Or an inflamed gland can **leak** stored hormone, as in subacute thyroiditis, and then uptake is low because TSH is suppressed and no new hormone is being made.

The {{graves|Graves}} pattern is diffuse uptake, a toxic adenoma is a single hot nodule, and toxic multinodular goiter shows patchy hot areas. A low-uptake scan in a thyrotoxic patient points to thyroiditis or to hormone taken as a pill.
Thionamides stop synthesis and work only when the gland is overproducing; they do nothing for a leaking gland, which recovers on its own while a beta-blocker controls symptoms.

grid.q: Which of these cause thyrotoxicosis with HIGH iodine uptake?
items: Iodine-driven hyperthyroidism in a nodular gland
Struma ovarii (uptake is in the pelvis, not the neck)
